task: Phase E Track B, B1 for N1 (conditional duration model), angles: performance-regression and latency-anomaly detection in APM/observability (Datadog Watchdog, Dynatrace, New Relic, academic APM anomaly detection); runtime prediction (CI build duration, database query latency, HPC job runtime). Question: does any model condition duration on declared workload and treat residuals as evidence of falsified records?
scope_note: Only public web pages, docs and papers were read. Nothing swarm-related was read or run. No agent transcripts generated. No paid API calls. PDFs fetched by WebFetch were converted to text with pypdf in the session scratchpad. That text is not committed, for copyright reasons. Every quote marked quote_method=pypdf_text was copied from that text; ligatures (fi, fl) are normalised and line-break hyphens joined. Quotes marked quote_method=webfetch_extract were returned verbatim by the WebFetch extraction model. They are close to verbatim, but a skeptic should re-open the URL before quoting them in the writeup.

sub_claims_as_defined.a: Duration-vs-expected-workload residuals as a fabrication signal in agent logs (PHASE_E_PROMPT.md, B1 bullet a; mechanism N1).
sub_claims_as_defined.b: corr(residual, output_size) as the discriminator between work-bound and generation-bound latency (PHASE_E_PROMPT.md, B1 bullet b; N1 second bullet).

bottom_line: VERDICT (a) = PARTIAL. The general idea is prior art outside agents, and one deployed system implements it: compare a reported duration with the declared workload and treat a mismatch as evidence that the record was falsified. BOINC CreditNew multiplies the client-reported elapsed time by the host's peak FLOPS and compares the result with the job's declared FLOP bound (wu.fpops_bound). If the product exceeds the bound, the claim is discarded and the host is put under suspicion, and the same page names 'falsifying benchmark scores or elapsed time' as the cheat. Sekar & Maniatis (CCSW 2011) propose, but do not build, a client that predicts resource consumption from workload features in its own execution log and checks it against the provider's report. The narrower combination is not found in any APM or runtime-prediction source checked: agent tool-call logs, generated (fabricated) results as the threat, and a baseline taken from within-session repeats of the same command.

VERDICT (b) = NOVEL within these angles, with one anecdotal precedent and one design caveat. No APM, performance-regression or runtime-prediction source uses corr(residual, output size) to tell work-bound from generation-bound latency. The closest item is anecdotal and in the agent domain. In anthropics/claude-code issue #67847 (open; opened 2026-06-12), users observe that fabricating turns are 'unusually long thinking-heavy responses (3.9k–5.5k output tokens, 60–90s)'. That is inline fabrication with no tool_use, so it is the N2 class, and it involves no residual and no correlation test. Caveat: honest data-movement latency also scales with bytes (LogGP's per-byte parameter G), so the sign of the correlation alone cannot separate I/O-bound honest calls from generated ones. See design_notes.

The mechanism's ancestor is old and TAKEN. Kelly (WORLDS 2005) models aggregate response time as a function of transaction mix and deems an interval anomalous when the observed value 'disagree[s] substantially' with the fit. TraceAnomaly (ISSRE 2020) conditions response time on call path. A third, Cherkasova et al. (DSN 2008), regresses CPU on transactions; it is known only through a secondary description and stays UNVERIFIED. In every one of them the log is trusted and a residual means a performance fault, never a forged record.

No APM product checked runs a workload-conditioned check on agent tool-call durations. Datadog Watchdog, Dynatrace Davis and New Relic baselines are conditioned on history, seasonality and endpoint identity (service, resource or method), not on payload or work size. Datadog's LLM Observability agent evaluations (Tool Selection, Tool Argument Correctness, Goal Completeness, Hallucination) are LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, and the docs mention no timing. Dynatrace MCP observability tracks 'request counts, durations, and error rates' and makes no claim to verify results.

A benchmark harness already embodies an active timing audit. In MLPerf Inference TEST04, LoadGen re-runs the workload with duplicate sample ids and fails the submission if it is more than 10% faster than the standard run, which would mean results were cached rather than computed. TEST01 and TEST09 check output consistency and output length against throughput cheating. These are active re-runs of a live system, not passive residuals on a past log, but the writeup should cite TEST04 as precedent for a 'faster than the declared work allows' check and for its pre-set 10% tolerance.

N1's baseline design is standard practice; cite it rather than claim it. Per-endpoint baselines are the APM default (Dynatrace per service method; Datadog per service/resource). Tsafrir, Etsion & Feitelson (TPDS 2007) predict job runtime as 'the runtimes of the last two jobs by the same user' and report that 'using recent data is more important than mining the history for similar jobs'. That is the same reasoning as N1's within-session same-command baseline.

a.taken_part: The concept of comparing a reported duration or resource use with what the declared workload predicts, and treating a large mismatch as evidence of a falsified record. It is deployed in BOINC CreditNew (reported elapsed time against the declared FLOP bound) and proposed in Sekar & Maniatis 2011 (predicted against reported consumption). The residual-as-anomaly mechanism is TAKEN in APM: Kelly 2005, TraceAnomaly 2020.
a.not_found_part: Applied to agent tool-call logs; the threat being a generated (fabricated) tool result rather than inflated billing or credit; a passive check on an existing transcript with no re-run and no instrumentation; a baseline from within-session repeats of the same command.
a.REASONING_not_citation: BOINC CreditNew does what (a) needs at its core. A party that is not trusted (the volunteer client) reports a duration. The server holds a declared workload for the job (fpops_est/fpops_bound). A reported duration the workload cannot explain is treated as cheating. It differs from (a) in four ways. (1) It checks a one-sided upper bound, catching inflated time, not a fitted residual. (2) The falsified field is the time itself, not the result content. (3) The declared workload is set by the project ahead of time, not inferred from same-command repeats. (4) It is volunteer computing, not agent logs. Sekar & Maniatis state the general principle for cloud billing as a proposal with no evaluation. The novelty of (a) must therefore be stated as transferring the check to agent tool logs, with a repeat-command baseline and a two-sided residual, and both should be cited.

b.scope_of_verdict: NOVEL only for the APM, performance-regression and runtime-prediction angles assigned to this task. The LLM-inference-latency and machine-generated-text angles belong to other B1 agents and may change it.
b.closest: anthropics/claude-code issue #67847, an anecdotal user observation that fabricating turns are long and output-token-heavy. MLPerf TEST09 checks output length against throughput cheating, but does no correlation.
b.REASONING_not_citation: No source in these angles regresses a duration residual on output size to decide which process (work or generation) produced the latency. The physical premise, that generation latency grows with output tokens, is common knowledge in LLM serving and is not novel; it belongs to the other angle. The discriminator as stated by N1 is not found. Design risk: LogGP-style models show that honest transfer, serialization and pagination latency is also proportional to bytes. corr>0 alone is therefore not diagnostic. The test should compare the fitted slope (seconds per KB) with a generation-rate prior, which is orders of magnitude slower per byte than honest I/O. That is reasoning, not a finding: Track A must measure it.

items.claim: B1(a): duration-vs-expected-workload residuals as a fabrication signal in agent tool logs
items.closest_work: BOINC CreditNew sanity check (deployed); Sekar & Maniatis, Verifiable Resource Accounting for Cloud Computing Services, CCSW 2011 (proposal)
items.what_it_does: BOINC: PFC(J) = T * peak_flops(J), where T is the client-reported elapsed time. If PFC(J) > wu.fpops_bound, the claim is replaced by a default and excluded from statistics, and the host is treated with suspicion. The page names falsified elapsed time as the cheat. Sekar & Maniatis: a client predicts resource consumption from workload features in its own tamper-resistant log and checks it against the provider's report.
items.what_it_does_not: Neither touches agent logs or fabricated tool results. BOINC uses a one-sided static bound, not a fitted residual, and the falsified field is time, not content. Sekar & Maniatis is a position paper with no implementation or evaluation of the prediction check. Neither uses within-session same-command repeats or output size.
items.deciding_citation: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/BOINC/boinc/CreditNew.md : "If `PFC(J) > wu.fpops_bound`, J is assigned a \"default PFC\" D and it's not used to update statistics."

items.claim: B1(b): corr(residual, output_size) discriminates work-bound from generation-bound latency
items.closest_work: anthropics/claude-code issue #67847 (anecdote: fabricating turns are long and output-heavy); MLPerf TEST09 (output length against throughput cheating)
items.what_it_does: #67847 reports fabricating turns of 3.9k–5.5k output tokens taking 60–90 s, and lists that as a pattern. TEST09 checks that the mean output token count stays near a reference mean, so that truncation cannot inflate throughput.
items.what_it_does_not: #67847 has no residual, no conditioning on the claimed work and no correlation test, and it concerns inline fabrication with no tool_use (the N2 class), not tool-call latency. TEST09 does not relate latency to length per call. No APM or runtime-prediction source uses a residual-vs-size correlation to discriminate between processes.
items.deciding_citation: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/67847 : "All fabricating turns: unusually long thinking-heavy responses (3.9k–5.5k output tokens, 60–90s), large context (133k–211k)."

items.claim: Mechanism ancestor: model latency as a function of the declared workload and flag large residuals as anomalies
items.closest_work: Kelly, Detecting Performance Anomalies in Global Applications, USENIX WORLDS 2005; also TraceAnomaly (Liu et al., ISSRE 2020) and Gow et al. 2013 (arXiv 1307.1743)
items.what_it_does: Fits the sum of response times per interval as sum_j alpha_j N_ij over the transaction-type counts, and deems intervals where the fit disagrees substantially anomalous. TraceAnomaly encodes response time per call path and scores traces by likelihood.
items.what_it_does_not: The logs are trusted. Anomalies are attributed to performance faults such as a misconfigured database connection pool. Nothing addresses forged, falsified or generated records, and nothing uses output size.
items.deciding_citation: https://static.usenix.org/events/worlds05/tech/full_papers/kelly/kelly_html/anomdet.html : "if the ŷᵢ agree closely with the corresponding yᵢ for most time intervals i, but disagree substantially for some i, deem the latter cases anomalous."

items.claim: A benchmark harness internally uses timing against the declared workload to detect results that were not actually computed
items.closest_work: MLPerf Inference compliance TEST04 (caching detection), with TEST01 and TEST09; Reddi et al., MLPerf Inference Benchmark, arXiv 1911.02549, section 'Result Review'
items.what_it_does: Runs the workload a second time with duplicate sample indices. If that run is significantly faster (more than 10%) than the run with unique samples, the system was caching instead of computing, and the submission fails.
items.what_it_does_not: It is an active audit that re-runs a live system under a changed workload. It is not a passive residual on a historical log, it does not apply to agent tool calls, and it does not use output size.
items.deciding_citation: https://github.com/mlcommons/inference/blob/master/compliance/TEST04/README.md : "Performance of TEST04 should not be faster than the standard performance run in a statistically significant way. To account for noise, TEST04 can be at most 10% faster than the standard performance run."

items.claim: An APM or LLM-observability product already embodies a workload-conditioned duration check on agent tool calls (the 'internally embodies' test)
items.closest_work: Datadog Watchdog and Datadog LLM Observability agent evaluations; Dynatrace Davis multidimensional baselining and MCP observability; New Relic anomaly detection
items.what_it_does: Watchdog builds latency, error-rate and hit baselines per service and resource from at least 2 weeks of history. Dynatrace builds median and p90 references per service method. New Relic builds seasonal history baselines. Datadog's agent evaluations (Tool Selection, Tool Argument Correctness, Goal Completeness, Hallucination) are LLM-as-a-judge. Dynatrace MCP observability records tool-call durations.
items.what_it_does_not: None of them conditions expected latency on the size of the claimed work or output, and none uses tool-call timing to judge whether a result is genuine. The docs fetched do not mention fabrication detection by timing.
items.deciding_citation: https://docs.datadoghq.com/watchdog/alerts/ : "Watchdog scans all services and resources to look for anomalies on the following metrics: Error rate, Latency, Hits (request rate)"

items.claim: N1 design element: baseline from recent repeats of the same command, not a global model
items.closest_work: Tsafrir, Etsion & Feitelson, Backfilling Using System-Generated Predictions Rather Than User Runtime Estimates, IEEE TPDS 2007; per-endpoint baselines in Dynatrace and Datadog
items.what_it_does: Predicts a job's runtime as the mean of the same user's last two completed jobs and finds that recency beats similarity mining. APM products baseline per service method or resource.
items.what_it_does_not: Used for scheduling and alerting, not for verification. The gap between the user's estimate and the actual runtime is treated as inaccuracy, never as falsification.
items.deciding_citation: https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~feit/papers/Pred07TPDS.pdf : "Notably, this is based on a very simple runtime predictor that just averages the runtimes of the last two jobs by the same user; counterintuitively, our results indicate that using recent data is more important than mining the history for similar jobs."

items.claim: Run duration (with command identity) as a feature separating two processes that generate records in CI
items.closest_work: Haben et al., Discerning Legitimate Failures From False Alerts: A Study of Chromium's Continuous Integration (Fair), arXiv 2111.03382
items.what_it_does: Uses run duration as the most important feature, with test command and code as static features, to classify a test-failure record as a legitimate failure or a flaky false alert (median 1.09 s against 0.41 s).
items.what_it_does_not: There is no adversary and no falsified records. It uses raw duration, not a residual against same-command repeats, and not output size.
items.deciding_citation: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.03382 : "the median duration of test executions is 1.09 seconds for legitimate failures, but only 0.41 seconds for false alerts."

items.claim: Premise behind (b): honest tool-call latency residuals are uncorrelated with output size
items.closest_work: LogGP (Alexandrov, Ionescu, Schauser, Scheiman, SPAA 1995): per-byte latency term G
items.what_it_does: Models message time as fixed overhead plus a per-byte term. Honest data movement is size-proportional.
items.what_it_does_not: It does not discuss fabrication. It is cited as a risk to (b), not as prior art: honest I/O-bound calls can also show residuals that correlate with size, so the slope magnitude (s/KB) has to be compared with a generation-rate prior.
items.deciding_citation: https://cs.ucsb.edu/research/tech-reports/1995-09 : "has one additional parameter, G, which captures the bandwidth obtained for long messages."

sources.title: BOINC wiki: CreditNew
passages: When a client finishes a job and reports its elapsed time T, we define `peak_flop_count(J)`, or PFC(J) as `PFC(J) = T * peak_flops(J)`

If `PFC(J) > wu.fpops_bound`, J is assigned a "default PFC" D and it's not used to update statistics. D is determined as follows: If app.min_avg_pfc is defined then `D = app.min_avg_pfc * wu.fpops_est` Otherwise `D = wu.fpops_est`
Host normalization mostly eliminates the incentive to cheat by claiming excessive credit (i.e., by falsifying benchmark scores or elapsed time)
One-time cheats. For example, claiming a PFC of 1e304. This is handled by the sanity check mechanism, which grants a default amount of credit and treats the host with suspicion for a while.
sources.does_not: One-sided upper bound only, so it catches inflated durations, not generated results. Result correctness is handled separately by replication and validators. No output-size term. It is not a fitted residual.
sources.note: The wiki page shows no date. Not established here when the sanity check was introduced.

sources.title: Verifiable Resource Accounting for Cloud Computing Services
sources.venue: ACM CCSW 2011 (the PDF file name says 2011CCSW)
passages: Verifiability here means that cloud customers can be assured that (a) their applications indeed physically consumed the resources they were charged for and (b) that this consumption was justified based on an agreed policy.

The first option is to use resource prediction. While such tools are motivated by provisioning or scheduling applications, they can also provide basic verification checks. For example, the client can extract key features of the workload from its own tamper-resistant execution log and check if the predicted resource consumption roughly matches the reports from the provider.
Resource prediction is challenging because workloads are hard to characterize and there are many hidden factors.
sources.does_not: Position paper. The prediction check is one paragraph under 'Relaxing provider assistance', with no implementation or evaluation. The party under suspicion is the cloud provider over-reporting consumption, not an agent fabricating results. No output-size discriminator.

sources.title: VeriCount: Verifiable Resource Accounting Using Hardware and Software Isolation
sources.authors: Shruti Tople, Soyeon Park, Min Suk Kang, Prateek Saxena
passages: both the cloud providers and the clients have the incentive to manipulate claims about resource usage.

leverages security features present in trusted computing solutions, such as Intel SGX, to measure user CPU time, memory, I/O bytes and network bandwidth while simultaneously detecting resource usage inflation attacks.
sources.does_not: Requires a TEE (SGX) witness, so it is instrumented. It does not predict expected consumption from the workload. Only the abstract was read; enough to classify it as instrumentation-based.

sources.authors: Richard Gow, Srikumar Venugopal, Pradeep Kumar Ray (UNSW)
passages: The first technique involved creating a resource consumption model of an application that, using regression, correlated processed transactions and consumed CPU time. The aim was to maintain a model that reflected resource consumption during normal operations. Significant changes in CPU resource consumption were then used to identify performance anomalies or application changes.
sources.does_not: Performance anomalies only. A grep for fraud|falsif|fabricat|forg|tamper|cheat|adversar|malicious finds nothing. The passage above describes Cherkasova et al. DSN 2008, which was not opened (see unverified).

sources.title: Pip: Detecting the Unexpected in Distributed Systems
sources.angle: academic APM: declared expectations against traces
sources.conditions_duration_on_declared_workload: declared static limits per task/path, not a workload model
passages: Pip allows programmers to express, in a declarative language, expectations about the system's communications structure, timing, and resource consumption.

Programmers can express upper and lower limits on the resources that any task, message, or path can consume. Pip defines several metrics, including real time, CPU time, number of context switches, and message size and latency.
sources.does_not: Finds bugs and performance problems in trusted, self-instrumented traces. The extractor reported no discussion of forged annotations.

sources.title: MLPerf Inference Benchmark
sources.treats_mismatch_as_falsification: treats 'faster than unique-sample run' as evidence of prohibited caching, i.e. results not computed
passages: In this test, results returned from the SUT to the LoadGen are logged randomly. The log is checked against the log generated in accuracy mode to ensure consistency.

The test has two parts: the first generates queries with unique sample indices, and the second generates queries with duplicate sample indices. It measures performance in each case. The way to detect caching is to determine whether the test with duplicate sample indices runs significantly faster than the test with unique sample indices.
sources.does_not: Active audit that requires re-running the system. Aggregate throughput, not per-call residuals. No output-size term.

design_notes_REASONING_not_findings: Prior art to cite in DESIGN.md for N1. Kelly 2005 for the residual-as-anomaly mechanism. BOINC CreditNew and Sekar & Maniatis 2011 for the check of declared work against reported duration as a test for falsification. MLPerf TEST04 for a harness-level 'too fast for the claimed work' audit with a 10% tolerance. Tsafrir 2007 for the recent same-key baseline. The claim should be scoped to agent tool-call logs plus a passive check plus a two-sided residual plus the output-size discriminator.

Direction. BOINC checks a one-sided upper bound (inflated time), while MLPerf TEST04 checks the lower side (too fast). A fabricated tool result can fail either way: a generated 'pytest' that returns faster than real execution, or a generated large output that takes longer than a real 'cat'. N1's residual test should be two-sided, or split by output size.

Risk for (b). Honest latency also has a per-byte term (LogGP G: transfer, serialisation, pagination, terminal rendering). Honest corr(residual, output_bytes) will be positive for I/O-heavy commands, so the sign alone cannot discriminate. Compare the fitted slope (s/KB) with a generation-rate prior, since LLM decoding at tens of tokens per second is roughly 1e3 to 1e5 times slower per byte than local I/O. Track A has to measure this; it is not established here.

Coverage interaction. Within-session repeats of the same command often return byte-identical output, which leaves output_bytes with no variance and corr undefined for that group. The discriminator needs repeats whose output sizes differ (for example 'git log', 'pytest -x' after edits). That bounds (b)'s coverage below the repeat-command rate N1 already reports.
